Du Ghana à Montréal, le voyage de Kwaben: From Ghana to Montréal, Kwabena's journey toward the LGBTQ+ community and acceptance
Kwabena a quitté le Ghana pour le Québec: Kwabena left Ghana for Quebec in early November, fleeing persecution because of his homosexuality.
<strong>Dans le brouhaha sympathique du: In the friendly buzz of a library café, we meet Kwabena Kaye-Essien, a 31-year-old Ghanaian who has settled in Montréal.
Kwabena a quitté le Ghana au début du mo: Kwabena left Ghana in early November 2023, fleeing persecution because of his homosexuality. He tells how he ended up on the other side of the world. Eager to share his story, he speaks animatedly for more than an hour about how he came to Quebec.
Kwabena a un sourire éclatant, une voix: Kwabena has a dazzling smile, a soft voice and kind eyes. “I'm someone who likes to talk, and everyone who likes to talk is my friend,” he says. But when we delve into his past, he quickly turns serious.
Kwabena se décrit comme quelqu’un « d’ho: Kwabena describes himself as “honest and frank,” which isn't always easy for a queer person in Ghana. In his view, the secrecy and contempt weighing on his community make it hard to feel truly at home even within his country's small LGBTQ+ community.
« Il existe une homophobie intériorisée,: “There is an internalized homophobia that comes from society and from the families we live in. Some people come from a very conservative religious background, and even though they are queer, they simply don't want to accept their orientation. They struggle with religion and their sexuality,” he explains.
Kwabena a grandi dans le village Huni Va: Kwabena grew up in the village of Huni Valley, in western Ghana. A member of the Akan ethnic group and the Fante tribe, he managed to hide his sexuality from his family until he finished secondary school in 2012. When she discovered he was gay, his mother began subjecting him to public humiliation and verbal abuse.
« J’ai vécu l’enfer avec ma mère. Elle p: “My mother put me through hell. She could insult me from morning till night,” he says.
Il connaît un peu de répit lorsqu’il dém: He found some respite when he moved to Accra, the country's capital, where he studied human resources management and business administration at university. His family thought he had “prayed for homosexuality to go away” during his studies.
Mais en 2021, des images en ligne le mon: But in 2021, online images of him in an LGBTQ+ safe space in Ghana resurfaced. His mother's abuse started up again, worse than before.
« Elle a même fini par me dire que j’éta: “She even ended up telling me I was a burden, that the money used to pay for my university studies, excuse my language, should have been used to build public toilets and that she would have had a better return on her investment,” he says, his eyes wide. “I got to a point where I considered suicide, because the constant insults, the name-calling and everything else really got to me,” he adds.
En quête de réconfort, Kwabena devient b: Seeking comfort, Kwabena began volunteering with a local LGBTQ+ rights organization in Accra. He eventually landed a job there as its finance director, a full-time position he held in 2021. The organization offers outreach activities, safer spaces and financial assistance to queer people.
« Au début, c’était vraiment génial. J’a: “In the beginning, it was really great. I felt like I was home and part of my community,” says Kwabena.
Mais la vie au sein de cette organisatio: But life within the organization was not without its difficulties. Its members have to go unnoticed to avoid persecution. Some, including Kwabena, lived at the headquarters. The place served as a living space, partly so the organization could remain secret.
En 2022, la police est informée de la pr: In 2022, police were tipped off about a trans woman outside the organization's premises. When questioned, she revealed that the house sheltered queer people, and police raided it. No charges were laid, because at the time, Ghanaian law only punished people caught in the act of non-heterosexual sex. Still, the residents began to fear further police action.
L’organisation apporte un soutien financ: The organization gave Kwabena financial and emotional support for a time. But the pressures of living together, working together and fighting for the survival of the community eventually wore down his efforts.
« Nous avons mêlé sentiments personnels: “We mixed personal feelings with professionalism, and our personal feelings can take over our professionalism. There were so many petty quarrels and arguments. How can we expect to be respected, tolerated and accepted if we are not united?” the young man laments.
Les conflits interpersonnels et les accu: Interpersonal conflicts and accusations of favouritism multiplied, and Kwabena ultimately left the organization last July. “What my mother did to me hurt, but what my community did to me hurt even more,” he sums up.‍
À court d’argent, Kwabena quitte son ref: Short on money, Kwabena left his refuge to move in with a friend. To make matters worse, an anti-LGBTQ+ bill was revived in Ghana's Parliament at the same time. “Everything related to queer identity is criminalized in this bill,” he explains.
Initialement présenté en 2021, le projet: First introduced in 2021, the bill, titled “<l1>Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values</l1>,” passed second reading in 2023.
Il prévoit notamment des peines de priso: Among other things, it provides for prison sentences for public displays of affection between same-sex partners, the dissolution of LGBTQ+ organizations and a “duty to report” LGBTQ+ rights advocacy activities.
« Si vous allez sur la page Instagram [d: “If you go on the Instagram page [of the LGBTQ+ rights organization], you'll see my photos. There are interviews of me on YouTube [about my work defending the rights of queer people]. The bill authorizes any citizen to report anyone suspected of being gay. It also gives your parents and your landlord the responsibility to ‘out’ you. Imagine your mother has said all kinds of things about you, has dishonoured you in public. Is she going to protect you? She'll surely prefer to protect the family as a whole, because if the authorities find out they didn't report you, they'll hold the family responsible,” he says.
Le projet de loi a été approuvé par le P: The bill was approved by Ghana's Parliament in February, after Kwabena left Ghana. The legislation still awaits the president's signature before it can come into force.
« Même avant l’adoption de ce projet de: “Even before this bill passed, there were many cases of blackmail, beatings, people being stabbed. Now people have a power legitimized by law to keep doing it,” he adds.
Kwabena a lui-même vécu du chantage, ce: Kwabena himself experienced blackmail, which hastened his departure from Ghana. He had invited over a man he had met on Grindr, a dating app for gay men. When his guest arrived, Kwabena saw that the man looked nothing like his Grindr profile. Having lost touch with the members of the LGBTQ+ rights group, he hadn't seen the warning they had sent on WhatsApp about this man, who was known to be a blackmailer. Kwabena believes what happened next could not have been avoided.
« Honnêtement, j’ai dû laisser [le maîtr: “Honestly, I had to let [the blackmailer] do whatever he wanted. Sex requires chemistry between two people, and you need some kind of connection to get there. But since I just lay there, doing nothing, he got frustrated. He told me to give him money so he would leave. I had spent all the money I had on rent, so I had to borrow money from my cousin to get him to go.”
Il raconte le tout d’une manière très fa: He recounts it all in a very matter-of-fact way, maintaining eye contact. His story takes a graver turn when he talks about the consequences of that encounter: “These blackmailers, if they don't get something out of you, they come back to cause more trouble. They extract a lot from you. Even if you give them everything you have, they end up outing you to the public. So I packed my bags and left.”
Découragé, sans le sou et épuisé, Kwaben: Discouraged, penniless and exhausted, Kwabena landed in Montréal on November 2, 2023. He had no money, but luckily he had a visa still valid for entering Canada and valuable connections from attending an AIDS prevention conference in Montréal in 2022.
Quand on lui demande de décrire son arri: When asked to describe his arrival in Montréal, his tone changes completely. He sits up straight and breaks into a wide smile. “You think your life is over, and then people welcome you, you meet extraordinary people… It's great! Oh my God, I love being here in Montréal,” he says, beaming.
« J’ai rencontré tellement de gens extra: “I've met so many extraordinary people!” says Kwabena.
C’est grâce à Kwame, un ami canadien d’o: It was thanks to Kwame, a Ghanaian-Canadian friend, that he found someone to host him temporarily. Kwame and he had met at the HIV Prevention Research Conference in 2022.
« Kwame m’a dit : “Je vais bloquer tous: “Kwame told me, ‘I'm going to block all my Ghanaian friends on my Facebook and post what you need.’ Luckily, five minutes later, someone replied that they could take me in,” he says.
Kwabena a exprimé sa profonde gratitude: Kwabena expressed deep gratitude toward his host, Emily, who put him up for free for six months, buying him a metro pass and other basic necessities. “We're a family now,” he says.
Il a rencontré un autre de ses amis les: He met another of his closest friends, Tony, through Grindr, an experience diametrically opposed to the one he had with his blackmailer. “Meeting Tony is also one of the best things that has happened to me here in Montréal,” he says happily. “His mother is Ghanaian and Akan, so he speaks our local language fluently and eloquently. We connected immediately.”
Depuis son arrivée, Kwabena a rencontré: Since arriving, Kwabena has met many other people through volunteering and going to Montréal's LGBTQ+ community centre. He volunteers for Aids Community Care Montreal, where he also sits on the board of directors, as well as for the Canadian Association for Education and Outreach, an LGBTQ2S+ organization.
« Je suis très en contact avec la commun: “I'm very connected to the LGBTQ2S+ community,” he says. Kwabena feels that he is now comfortable in his own skin. “I wake up every day without thinking about what someone will say about me, how I have to dress, how I have to walk so I won't seem so effeminate,” he explains.
Kwabena espère que son copain pourra bie: Kwabena hopes his boyfriend will soon be able to join him in Canada. “The only thing I miss is my boyfriend. My God, I miss him so, so, so much! I wish he were here with me!” he says.
Les deux se sont rencontrés en novembre: The two met in November 2022 at an art festival in Ghana and have been together ever since. “For me, it was truly love at first sight. In fact, it's my first relationship that has lasted more than six months. I hope we can soon make our relationship official and legal,” he says.
Le parcours de Kwabena n’est pas encore: Kwabena's journey is not over yet. He has received his work permit but hasn't yet found stable employment. He has gone over his story with a lawyer in preparation for the hearing he must attend to obtain refugee status. For him, the fight is worth it.
« Je ne dirais pas que je suis <em>libre: “I wouldn't say I'm free… but I feel like I'm in my comfort zone. I feel like I'm in a place where I'm accepted and where I can be whatever I want to be,” says the young man happily.
